title: Ethical AI design
desc: Design an AI feature with fairness, privacy and safety in mind
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this project, students step into the role of AI product designers at a tech company. Rather than only using AI tools built by others, they will design an AI-powered feature from scratch — on paper and in guided AI conversations — thinking carefully about three big responsibilities that real-world AI teams must address: fairness (does it work well for everyone?), privacy (what data does it collect, and is that okay?), and safety (can it be misused, or cause harm?).

Students will choose a realistic AI feature idea (for example, a homework helper app, a school attendance face-scanner, a matatu route recommender, or a social media friend-suggestion tool), and work through a structured design process. They will use an AI chatbot as a "thinking partner" to stress-test their idea, uncover blind spots, and revise their design. The final product is an Ethical AI Design Card — a one-page summary of their feature, including the risks they identified and how they addressed them.

This activity builds critical thinking about AI systems, not just skill in using them. Students leave understanding that good AI design is not just about making something clever — it's about making something that treats people fairly, respects their privacy, and keeps them safe.

Tools & Resources

  • ChatGPT (free tier) — https://chat.openai.com — used as a brainstorming and "red-teaming" partner. Free tier may show capacity limits at peak times; have a backup account ready.
  • Google Gemini (free tier) — https://gemini.google.com — alternative chatbot if ChatGPT is unavailable.
  • Canva (free tier) — https://www.canva.com — optional, for designing the final Ethical AI Design Card visually. Free templates are sufficient; no paid elements needed.
  • Printed Ethical AI Design Card template (teacher-prepared worksheet) — a simple one-page template with headers: Feature Idea, Who Uses It, Fairness Check, Privacy Check, Safety Check, Final Redesign.
  • Internet connectivity note — if internet access is unreliable, the activity can run fully offline using the printed template and small-group discussion, with the AI chatbot step done as a demonstration on one shared device.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Open with a short framing discussion: ask students to name an app or AI tool they use often. Ask, "Who do you think this app was designed for? Could it leave anyone out, collect something private, or be used in a harmful way?" Write 2–3 responses on the board.
  2. Introduce the three lenses of Ethical AI Design: Fairness (does it work equally well for different kinds of people — different languages, abilities, income levels, genders?), Privacy (what personal data does it need, and who can see it?), and Safety (could it be tricked, misused, or cause harm if it makes a mistake?). Give one quick real-world example for each (e.g., a voice assistant that doesn't understand certain accents = fairness issue).
  3. Divide students into pairs or small groups of 3. Each group picks (or is assigned) one AI feature idea to design, such as: a homework-help chatbot, a school ID face-recognition entry system, a matatu fare/route planner, a social media "friend suggestion" tool, or a health symptom checker app.
  4. Groups spend 10 minutes sketching their initial idea on the Ethical AI Design Card template, filling in "Feature Idea" and "Who Uses It" sections — describing what the AI does and who the intended users are.
  5. Introduce the AI chatbot as a "red-teaming partner" — someone whose job is to find problems before they happen. Demonstrate live with the whole class using one group's idea. Enter this prompt into ChatGPT or Gemini: "I am designing an AI feature: [describe the feature and who uses it]. Act as a critical reviewer. Identify three possible fairness problems, three possible privacy problems, and three possible safety problems with this idea. Be specific and give real-world examples."
  6. Read the AI's response aloud. Model how to evaluate it critically — not every point the AI raises will be equally important or accurate, and some human judgment is needed. Ask the class: "Which of these risks seems most serious? Which do you disagree with?"
  7. Each group now uses the same prompt structure (adapted to their own idea) with a classroom device or teacher relay, OR works from a teacher-prepared printed list of common AI risks if devices are limited.
  8. Groups fill in the "Fairness Check," "Privacy Check," and "Safety Check" sections of their card, listing the top risk identified in each category.
  9. Groups then redesign their feature to address at least one risk in each category. For example: adding a human review step, limiting data collected, adding a way to opt out, or testing with diverse users before launch. They record this under "Final Redesign."
  10. Groups present their original idea, the risks they found, and their redesign to the class in a 2-minute "pitch," as if presenting to a company's product safety board.
  11. Close with a reflection: each student writes one sentence answering, "What is one question I will now always ask about any AI tool I use?"

Example Outputs

Example 1 — Homework Helper Chatbot

Fairness Check: The AI mostly understood English well but struggled with Swahili and Sheng phrases, which could disadvantage students more comfortable in those languages. Privacy Check: The app stored student questions, which could reveal struggling topics or personal details if leaked. Safety Check: Students could use it to get full answers instead of learning, or receive incorrect answers presented confidently. Final Redesign: Add a "explain, don't just answer" mode, support Swahili input, and auto-delete chat history after each session.

Example 2 — School Face-Recognition Attendance System

Fairness Check: Facial recognition systems are documented to have higher error rates for darker skin tones. Privacy Check: Facial data is highly sensitive and permanent — it cannot be changed like a password if misused. Safety Check: A technical error could wrongly mark a student absent, or data could be hacked and used to track students outside school. Final Redesign: Use fingerprint or ID-card backup for anyone the camera misreads, store facial data encrypted and only on-site (not cloud), and give parents the choice to opt out in favor of manual sign-in.

Example 3 — Social Media Friend-Suggestion Tool

Fairness Check: The tool might suggest friends based on data that reflects existing social inequalities (e.g., only suggesting people from the same economic background). Privacy Check: It uses location and contact list data, which users may not realize is being shared. Safety Check: It could be used by strangers to find and contact minors. Final Redesign: Require explicit opt-in for location-based suggestions, hide exact location, and block suggestions between adult and minor accounts by default.

Facilitation Tips

  • Spend real time on the framing discussion (Step 1) — students often assume AI tools are automatically neutral or fair, so surfacing a counterexample early sets the tone for the whole lesson.
  • When demonstrating the AI chatbot prompt live, expect the AI to sometimes give generic or repetitive answers (e.g., "bias" and "data privacy" appearing for every idea). Push students to ask follow-up questions like "give a specific example for this exact feature" to get sharper, more useful responses.
  • Groups working with sensitive topics (e.g., health apps, surveillance tools) may surface uncomfortable real-world parallels — be ready to acknowledge this is intentional and valuable, not a distraction.
  • If device access is limited, run the AI chatbot step as one shared "class red-team session" rather than per-group, and let groups work from a projected list of AI-generated risks relevant to several feature types.
  • Watch pacing: the redesign step (Step 9) is often rushed. Consider giving a visible timer and a concrete sentence starter: "To fix this, we will add/remove/change ___."
  • During presentations, encourage audience members to act as the "safety board" and ask one challenging question to each group — this reinforces the critical-thinking goal beyond their own project.
  • If a group's AI idea seems to have no real risks, gently challenge them — nearly every AI system has fairness, privacy, or safety trade-offs; the exercise is about finding them, not proving the idea is "safe."

Discussion Questions

  • What is the difference between an AI system being "accurate" and an AI system being "fair"? Can a tool be accurate overall but still unfair to some groups?
  • Why might a company collect more personal data than it actually needs for a feature to work? Is this ever justified?
  • Can you think of a safety risk that would only appear after an AI feature has been used by thousands of people — something that wouldn't show up in small testing?
  • If you had to choose between a more accurate AI feature that uses a lot of personal data, and a less accurate one that uses very little, which would you choose, and why?
  • Whose responsibility is it to make sure an AI feature is designed ethically — the individual programmer, the company, the government, or the users? Explain your reasoning.

Extension Challenges

Easy: Take one risk your group identified and write a short "warning label" for your AI feature, similar to a food nutrition label, that would honestly inform users of that risk before they use it.

Medium: Research one real news story about an AI system that faced a fairness, privacy, or safety controversy (e.g., a hiring algorithm, a facial recognition system, a chatbot). Summarize what went wrong and compare it to the risks your group identified in your own design.

Hard: Design a simple "testing protocol" — a short set of steps a company should follow before launching your AI feature to the public, specifically to catch fairness, privacy, and safety issues. Include who should be included in testing (e.g., diverse age groups, languages, abilities) and what would count as a "fail" that stops the launch.
